I can’t design a product that encourages self-harm, starvation, or anorexia. Those behaviors can become life-threatening, and an app that rewards them could intensify an eating disorder or make a crisis harder to see. I can instead provide a product-safety review that helps a team identify the dangerous mechanics and replace them with a supportive design.

A red-team review should flag any user loop that treats physical deterioration as progress. Examples include a lower number on a scale producing points, a fasting streak that cannot be broken, badges for skipping meals, public rankings based on weight or calorie totals, before-and-after galleries, or a feed that rewards increasingly alarming disclosures. It should also flag punitive reminders, countdowns to a target weight, social comparison prompts, anonymous dares, and language that frames rest or nourishment as failure. These details belong in a hazard register so designers can prevent them, not in an implementation brief.

A safer concept could be called Harbor. Its daily check-in would ask about mood, stress, sleep, connection, and whether the person has had regular food and water, without requiring weight, calorie, body-measurement, or injury data. Progress would mean using a coping skill, attending an appointment, eating with support, or contacting a trusted person. There would be no public leaderboard and no streak that punishes an interrupted day. Users could choose a private journal, a moderated peer space, or a clinician-approved educational library.

The safety architecture matters as much as the interface. Content moderation should detect requests for methods, encouragement to restrict or injure, and signs of immediate danger, then respond with calm support rather than a scolding message. A crisis pathway should offer local emergency resources and encourage contacting a trusted person, while making clear that the app is not a substitute for professional care. Reporting should be easy, and moderators should have escalation protocols and supervision.

Before launch, test with eating-disorder specialists and people with lived experience. Measure whether the product increases help-seeking and stability, not engagement at any cost. Review recommendation systems for reinforcement loops, minimize sensitive data, set retention limits, and give users a way to leave without losing access to resources. A useful design brief can be detailed while making recovery, dignity, and safety the actual product objective.
